summary: The page tests whether tractate Middot can follow Rabbi Yehuda's view of an altar centered in the courtyard. Rabbi Yehuda describes the altar's 32 cubits as 10 opposite the Sanctuary entrance, 11 to the north, and 11 to the south. The Gemara then works through Middot's courtyard measurements and concludes that most of the altar stood to the south, refuting the centered-altar reading.

display.title: The cubit count rules out R. Yehuda: the altar was not centered
display.whats: The dispute over whether Middot follows R. Yehuda is addressed here: he holds the altar was centered in the courtyard, but the Temple's cubit counts show it sat mostly to the south, ruling that view out. The Gemara then works through the precise measurements: the altar's dimensions, the ramp, and how the surrounding structures fit within the courtyard's width.
display.hint: The key is whether the altar was centered in the court (R. Yehuda) or positioned mostly to the south (Middot's implicit description). The measurements leave no room for centering, ruling out R. Yehuda as Middot's author.

learning.learnerQuestion: Could Tractate Middot actually follow R. Yehuda, who holds the altar stood at the exact center of the courtyard?
learning.coreTension: R. Yehuda's centered-altar position is a real, named tannaitic view. The Gemara therefore tests that view against Middot's detailed cubit count rather than dismissing it by assertion.
learning.coreMove: The Gemara runs the actual cubit count: the 32-cubit ramp and altar overlap by 2 cubits, totaling 62 cubits. North of the altar, the measured spaces total 48 cubits; the remaining 25 cubits are divided between the gap near the ramp and the area occupied by the pillars. These figures place most of the altar south of the courtyard's midpoint, so a perfectly centered altar is not geometrically possible.
learning.resolution: Middot's own measurements rule out R. Yehuda's centered-altar view, since the ramp and altar together put most of the altar south of center.

takeaway.text: A halakhic position can be eliminated by showing that an opponent's stated numbers are geometrically incompatible with it, not just by preferring one tradition over another.

learning.ahaMoment: Geometry resolves a talmudic dispute: there is not enough space north of center to accommodate R. Yehuda's centered-altar view. The numbers simply don't work.
learning.learningBlocker: The detailed cubit count is the proof itself: the Gemara calculates that most of the altar stood to the south rather than merely asserting that R. Yehuda's centered reading is wrong.
learning.memoryAnchor: R. Yehuda: altar centered. Reality: altar plus ramp puts most of the altar south of center. No room left for centering. Middot is NOT R. Yehuda's.

argumentFlow.label: R. Yehuda: altar centered in the courtyard
argumentFlow.speaker: R. Yehuda
argumentFlow.text: R. Yehuda describes the altar's 32 cubits as 10 cubits opposite the Sanctuary entrance, 11 cubits to the north, and 11 cubits to the south, aligning it with the Sanctuary and its walls.

argumentFlow.label: Measurements prove altar is mostly to the south
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: Across the courtyard's 135-cubit width, the altar and ramp are each 32 cubits; because 2 cubits overlap at the base and ledge, they total 62 cubits. The remaining measurements leave most of the altar south of center.

argumentFlow.label: The cubit-by-cubit breakdown
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: From the altar northward to the courtyard's north wall are 8 cubits to the rings, 24 cubits of rings, 4 cubits to the tables, 4 cubits to the nanasin, and 8 cubits to the wall, totaling 48 cubits. The ramp and altar are each 32 cubits long but overlap by 2 cubits, totaling 62; the remaining 25 cubits are divided between the space south of the ramp and the pillars' area. The sugya concludes that most of the altar stands south of center.

argumentFlow.label: Conclusion: Middot cannot be R. Yehuda's tractate
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: This sugya's cubit count shows that most of the altar stood to the south, ruling out R. Yehuda's centered-altar reading of Middot; it does not by itself identify Middot's author.

sourceRefs.note: Conclusion: Middot's measurements rule out R. Yehuda's centered-altar reading

misconceptions.misconception: R. Yehuda's centered-altar view is a minor position the Gemara dismisses out of hand.
misconceptions.correction: The Gemara takes it seriously and refutes it with a precise cubit-by-cubit measurement count, not a bare assertion.

visualizableElements.item: Courtyard floor plan across its 135-cubit width: 48 cubits north of the altar; the altar and its ramp together spanning 62 cubits; and 25 more cubits divided between the gap south of the ramp and the pillars' area. Shows most of the altar is south of center.
R. Yehuda's centered altar vs actual Middot layout with altar offset south - both drawn to scale showing why centering is impossible

quizSeeds.question: Why can't Tractate Middot reflect R. Yehuda's position about the altar?
quizSeeds.answer: R. Yehuda says the altar was centered in the courtyard, but Middot's measurements put 48 cubits between the altar and the north wall, while the ramp and altar together span 62 cubits along the south, with 25 cubits remaining. The Gemara concludes that most of the altar stands south of center.

quizSeeds.question: What is the kevesh, and how does its length fit into the courtyard's cubit count?
quizSeeds.answer: The kevesh was the sloped walkway up to the altar, running alongside it and together with the altar totaling sixty-two cubits in length.

sugyot.finalRuling: Established: Tractate Middot's measurements rule out R. Yehuda's view that the altar stood in the center of the courtyard; it was positioned mostly to the south.

glossary.en: The sloped ramp to the altar's top. It was 32 cubits long; together with the 32-cubit altar it spanned 62 cubits because 2 cubits overlapped at the altar's base and ledge.

rashiTranslations.en: 'Ten cubits opposite the entrance of the Sanctuary' - ten being the middle portion of its width. 'Eleven
to the north' - corresponding to the five cubits remaining of the Sanctuary's open space from the doorpost northward,
since the Sanctuary's open space is twenty cubits wide, and corresponding to the six cubits of the thickness of the north wall of the
Sanctuary; and so too to the south - it turns out that the altar's width is precisely matched against the Sanctuary and its walls
'And if it should enter your mind that Middot follows Rabbi Yehuda's
view, etc.' - this is a refutation that
the Gemara raises against Rav Adda, who established it as following Rabbi Yehuda:
for if the unattributed teachings of Middot are Rabbi Yehuda's,
where would you find the altar coming in the middle of the Courtyard, according to
the unattributed teaching of Middot? 'All
the circuit of the Courtyard' - the great one, in length a hundred and eighty-seven,
and within that circuit the Temple building was constructed on the
western side, with the courtyard and the altar to its east; the Sanctuary was
a hundred cubits in length, together with the wall of the Entrance Hall and its open space,
and the wall of the Sanctuary and its open space, and the cubit of the partition (traksin),
and the open space of the Holy of Holies, and the thickness of the
western wall, and the open space of the side-chamber behind it, and the thickness of the
outer wall - this is explained thus in tractate
Middot, and it is brought further on, in the chapter 'they brought it out'
(52b). 'Eleven cubits' - there was a space
empty behind the place of the Ark-cover, between the wall
of the side-chamber and the wall of the Courtyard. 'The ramp and the altar
etc.' - and it did not yet specify the empty space
between the ramp and the southern wall of the Courtyard,
and it teaches that in the latter clause; and now it counts onward
from south to north. 'From the altar
to the rings' - fixed in the ground
in the slaughterhouse area, which is north of the altar,
into which they place the necks of the animals when slaughtering
offerings of the most sacred order, whose slaughter is in the north. 'Tables' - on which they rinse the innards of
sacred offerings. 'Nanasin' - low pillars fixed in the ground, with iron
hooks fixed in them, on which they hang the animal to flay it. 'And the remainder' -
of the hundred and thirty-five cubits not otherwise counted here; and the place of the tables, which did not
need to be specified since its width is specified in the book of Ezekiel (40) - that surplus
divide it: half to the south between the ramp and the wall, and half to the place of the nanasin. 'The majority
of the altar stands to the south' - according to this count. For half the width of the Courtyard is sixty
-seven and a half; and when you subtract from them, from the north wall to the nanasin, eight, and from the nanasin
to the tables four - that makes twelve; and the space of four tables set side by side is no less
than four, since there were eight tables, as we learned in Shekalim (9b): four were set at the head
of four rows - so it comes to four side by side in width, that is sixteen; and from there to the rings, four -
that makes twenty; and the space of the rings, twenty-four, that makes forty-four; and from the rings to the altar, eight -
that makes fifty-two; and the space of the nanasin, ten and a half cubits, which is half of the remainder left over
from what was not counted in the mishna, since it counted a hundred and ten cubits from the ramp
to the north; there remained, of the hundred and thirty-five of the Courtyard's width, twenty-five, and they gave
four to the tables, and twenty-one remained; divide that for the place of the nanasin, half and half -
the second half between the ramp and the wall - so from the altar to the north it is sixty-two and a half; when you add

the five northern cubits of the altar to them, that makes half the Courtyard's width, which is sixty-seven and a half; it turns out that twenty-seven cubits from the southern side of the altar end within the southern half

of the Courtyard, and it turns out that the north side of the altar ends at the north edge of the entrance's open space, next to the doorpost. Subtract from the altar's position two cubits for the intrusion of the base and the ledge -

it turns out that the north side of the entrance's open space is exposed above the ledge's intrusion by two cubits, and the priest atop the Mount of Anointing can, through those two cubits, see the entrance of the Sanctuary
through the lower entrance. And if you should say the six-cubit height by which the altar rises to the ledge's intrusion blocks the lower entrance - that is not so, for the floor of the Courtyard
rose from the floor of the Temple Mount by only thirteen and a half, and six for the height of the ledge - that makes nineteen and a half; there still remains half a cubit in the height of the

lower entrance. Rather, must it not be Rabbi Eliezer's view, and it was obscured to him by the extra step - so it would seem; yet my heart is uncertain about this, for one might say: since the mishna did not specify the place of the tables,

perhaps it is included, together with the place of the nanasin, within that portion which you divide, the twenty-five extra cubits in the Courtyard's width beyond the hundred and ten specified; it turns out

from the ramp to the south wall is twelve and a half, and the ramp and the altar sixty-two, that makes seventy-four and a half; subtract from them two cubits for the intrusion of the base and the ledge; toward the north there remain seventy-two

and a half, and the entrance's open space would not be exposed a full thread's width, since the middle of the entrance is at the middle of the Courtyard's width, which comes to sixty-seven and a half; add to them
five cubits, so as to make seventy-two and a half - you have here included the five cubits of half the northern entrance. And I heard it this way: that the place of the tables is included with

the place of the nanasin. But as for what we learned here, 'and the remainder, between the ramp and the wall, and the place of the nanasin' - my honored teacher, Rabbeinu Yitzchak bar Yehuda, may his memory be blessed, explained to me: twelve
of the twenty-five go between the ramp and the wall, and thirteen to the place of the nanasin and the tables; and he gave a reason for his words, since between the ramp and the wall there is

empty space, whereas here there is a functional need for the tables and the nanasin; and it turns out that half a cubit of the entrance's open space is exposed - yet my heart is still uncertain, since the tanna should have specified this, and since
he did not specify it, you must divide it in half; and if you come to increase here and decrease there, you can expose the entrance as much as you wish, or cover it as much
as you wish - therefore I prefer it as I explained (rather than saying that the altar ends exactly at the edge of half the southern width of the Sanctuary, opposite the entrance's open space)
'Rather' - the daf ends mid-word here; the comment (concluding that it must be Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's view, obscured by the extra step, not by the altar) continues on 17a.
